node.name: Advanced Search Techniques
node.descriptionText: Learn skills to research like a librarian, including how to use "advanced search" techniques to find books and articles in Quicksearch.
node.descriptionHtml:
Learn skills to research like a librarian, including how to use "advanced search" techniques to find books and articles in Quicksearch. Join us for 30-minutes and get a step ahead for coursework and research projects!

Attendees will learn how to:

  • navigate to distinct resource types in Quicksearch (books, articles, etc.)

  • use filters (subject, author, discipline) to find more relevant results

  • identify Advanced Search features

  • broaden and narrow search results using operators AND, OR, and NOT

Audience: Undergraduate students. Graduate students are also welcome.

Students interested in this workshop might also be interested in “First Steps with Zotero” and "Demystifying the Literature Review." For individual support, reach out to your Personal Librarian or Subject Specialist Librarian.

Any student who attends at least 3 library workshops this semester will be eligible to receive a Yale Library tote bag! Learn more about the Workshop Incentive Program.

node.name: An Introduction to Mixed-Effects Models for Hierarchical Data
node.descriptionText:
Do you have some sort of “grouping” in your data? Have heard that you might need to control for within-group variation but don’t really know what that means? Your PI said “use a mixed-effects model” but you don’t know where to start? Come to this workshop! 

The workshop will be offered primarily in R, but will provide multiple languages of worked code examples. During the workshop, we will take participants through the process of identifying non-independence in data, fitting a model to deal with that non-independence, and then performing inference on the result. We will focus on: 

- Defining fixed versus random effects and their respective usage Identifying and checking assumptions (and common mis-specifications) in mixed-effects models.
- Discussing and testing the utility of the various forms that random effects can take.
- Fitting, assessing, and visualizing mixed-effects models in R General strategies for non-independence 

This workshop is intended for those with some introductory knowledge of statistics, who have used and understand classic linear regression, and have a working version of R installed on their computer.

node.name: Daily Worship at Marquand Chapel
node.descriptionText:
Join us at 11:30am in Marquand Chapel for our daily worship.

Worship in Marquand often draws on a wide variety of inherited Christian traditions, with the worship of many denominations being represented. Beyond that, though, we also pay attention to the rising number of people in Western society who have a lively interest in spirituality but feel no connection to traditional forms of church and worship. So Marquand is also actively engaged in original, creative, and experimental forms of worship, both for committed Christians and for those exploring the faith.

node.name: CLIMATES - Who Bears the Burden? Climate Change, Rural Agriculture, and Energy Transitions in India
node.descriptionText: What does climate change look like through the eyes of rural farming communities in India, and can agricultural waste become part of the solution? Join Abhinaya Polaka (MESc ’27), a Three Cairns Climate Scholar at the Yale School of the Environment, as she shares insights from her fieldwork in South India. Drawing on conversations with farming households and women in rural communities, this talk explores how the physical impacts of climate change are affecting rural livelihoods. Abhinaya will also share insights into the potential of crop waste and biomass-based energy systems to provide cleaner cooking alternatives, reduce energy burdens, and create economic opportunities for rural communities.

node.name: Leaders in Public Health featuring Dr. Meena Seshamani
node.descriptionText:
Join Dean Megan Ranney and Dr. Meena Seshamani, Maryland's Secretary of Health, for a fireside chat.

From the operating room to the White House and now the state of Maryland’s cabinet, Dr. Meena Seshamani, MD, PhD, has built a career founded on making health care more accessible, affordable, and equitable. As Maryland’s secretary of health, and the former deputy administrator and director of the Center for Medicare at CMS, she has helped lead impactful work on vaccine access, rural health, drug pricing, value-based care, and insurance reform.

In this conversation, Dr. Seshamani will reflect on translating policy into meaningful impact in people’s lives, the promise of innovative health care payment models, and what it takes to pursue lasting public health reform in a changing political landscape.

The Leaders in Public Health Series is open to active Yale community members only for in-person attendance. The general public is welcome and encouraged to participate via the Zoom link provided. Thank you for your understanding.

node.name: Seeing the Big Picture: Using Deep Learning to Understand the Land Implications of Energy Systems at Scale, CIE Digital Economy and the Environment Series
node.descriptionText:
Estimates of the direct land area required by energy technologies began as rough approximations built on limited data from literature.  Methods have rapidly advanced in the past decade—from supervised classification to deep learning of earth observation imagery—enabling a greater understanding of the land implications of energy decisions across spatial and temporal scales.
 
Professor Sarah Jordaan of McGill University will cover this progression, up to new research applying deep learning models to quantify direct land use by solar, wind, hydroelectric and nuclear projects as well as coal- and gas-fired electricity. Deep learning applied to more than 500,000 earth observation images in the western United States produced land inventories for 719 solar photovoltaic facilities, 318 wind farms (15,871 turbines), and more than 100,000 natural gas production wells, complemented by manual delineation of aerial imagery for 594 hydropower plants, 42 coal-fired power plants, 8 concentrated solar plants, and 3 nuclear power projects. Prof. Jordaan will explore what these new techniques mean for understanding the land implications of energy transitions across spatial and temporal scales. Quantified using consistent methods, findings illuminate how new techniques enable us to “see the big picture” in support of a more environmentally sustainable energy future.

Dr. Jordaan is an Associate Professor of Industrial Ecology and Life Cycle Assessment in the Department of Civil Engineering and the Trottier Institute for Sustainability in Engineering and Design at McGill University. Her research applies industrial ecology tools and innovation systems to support a sustainable, low-carbon energy future. 

This lecture is part of the Center for Industrial Ecology's Digital Economy and the Environment Lecture series. Professor Jordaan's presentation will be in person and also available via zoom. It is free and open to the public. For those who are local, lunch will be available in room 319.

node.name: Dissertation Writing as Practice Series (Session 4): 11/17
node.descriptionText:
This series provides dissertation writers with the structure, resources, and creative outlets to design and maintain a sustainable approach to writing. We will explore effective practices for pacing your dissertation writing while helping you overcome common writing blocks and find balance in your writing life. During each weekly live workshop session, we will engage with a relevant theme, discuss your writing practice and progress, and complete low-stakes reflective and creative activities to build your writing momentum. Invigorated by poetry, art, and other creative inspirations, and supported through discussion boards and supplementary resources, we will help you craft a writing practice to help you maintain, and even enjoy, a PhD writing life. 

As part of the resources offered in this series, students will receive access to tutorials on how to try Scrivener, a software program for organizing writing and brainstorming. Students who attend at least four of the six sessions will receive a free, lifetime Scrivener license.

The weekly session themes are:  

1. Time Management and Dissertation Planning (10/27)
2. Crafting a Holistic Dissertation Writing Practice (11/3)
3. Working through Distractions and Procrastination (11/10)
4. Writing through Imposter Stress (11/17)
5. Hanging up on Perfectionism and Demoralization (12/1)
6. Assessing Process & Progress + Long-View Spring Semester Planning (12/8)

Intended Audience:  ABD PhD students from all disciplines who have begun writing their dissertation.

node.name: Geospatial CoP: Beyond the AI Hype - Build, Experiment, and Explore with GeoAI
node.descriptionText:
Curious about AI but ready to do more than chat with it? Dive into GeoAI, where artificial intelligence meets maps and spatial data, in this two-hour, hands-on workshop. Using ArcGIS Pro, you’ll experiment with GeoAI, create your own embeddings, and explore transfer learning to adapt an existing deep learning model rather than start from scratch. Through guided activities, you’ll build on each step, moving from your first experiment toward a connected GeoAI workflow. Whether you’re brand-new to GIS or already making maps, bring your curiosity and get ready to try something new. No GIS or AI experience required.

Brian Baldwin will also be available for 30 minutes after the workshop to answer any questions or offer advice on your individual projects.

node.name: A Conversation with Judge Dale Ho (S.D.N.Y)
node.descriptionText:
Judge Dale Ho sits on the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, where he has served since August 2023. Before joining the bench, he spent a decade leading the ACLU’s Voting Rights Project, overseeing its voting rights litigation nationwide and arguing twice before the U.S. Supreme Court, including the challenge to the 2020 census citizenship question. His earlier career included the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and Fried Frank, and clerkships with Judge Barbara Jones of the SDNY and Judge Robert Smith of the New York Court of Appeals. Judge Ho is a graduate of Princeton and Yale Law School (‘05).

Lunch will be provided.
Yale Law School community only.

node.name: LPE Workshop Series: Electricity and Energy with Professor Shelley Welton
node.descriptionText:
Please join us for the sixth session of the LPE Fall Workshop Series, Economic Governance in a Post-Neoliberal Age: Networks, Platforms, and Utilities (NPU) Law and Other Approaches. The session will be Tuesday, November 17th, from 12:10-1:30pm. Professor Shelley Welton will discuss NPU approaches to regulating electricity markets and energy governance. 

More on the Workshop Series:
Rapid technological and economic changes, political uncertainty, and climate change have supercharged longstanding challenges associated with concentrated private power across politics and the economy, raising new and urgent questions for the future of economic governance and our democracy. At the heart of many of these challenges lie industries known as networks, platforms, and utilities (NPUs)—economic sectors crucial for the functioning of the broader economy, such as finance, energy, communications, and transportation. The NPU speaker series will host distinguished scholars as they present their research and new perspectives on tools to regulate NPU industries from finance to AI to energy.

node.name: Wright-Ingraham Institute’s Field Workshop 2027 Info Session
node.descriptionText:
Applications are now open for the Wright-Ingraham Institute’s Field Workshop 2027, a three-week advanced fellowship for graduate students and early-career practitioners from any field. The program brings together a cohort representing diverse disciplines and knowledge systems to grow as integrative thinkers and doers.

Traveling through the San Luis Valley in southern Colorado and into the Taos Plateau in northern New Mexico, fellows learn alongside regional partners and undertake projects addressing local land and water challenges. Building on WII’s fifty-year history of field-based education, fellows learn to integrate different ways of knowing to develop better questions and insights into complex challenges.
